The WHO Health Emergencies Programme has been actively responding to numerous natural disasters, man-made disasters, armed conflicts, and infectious disease outbreaks, including pandemics. Experience has shown that outbreaks of diseases such as Ebola and Marburg, among other viral hemorrhagic fevers, will continue to occur. 8. It is crucial for Member States to enhance their capacity for preparedness, readiness, and response to emerging threats and outbreaks. Strong infection prevention and control (IPC) programs and response activities are essential for providing safe patient care and protecting healthcare workers. 9. IPC plays a vital role in health emergency readiness and response, ultimately saving lives. This guideline provides IPC recommendations specifically for Ebola and Marburg disease outbreaks, focusing on healthcare facilities while also considering community health delivery settings. 10. Member States, decision-makers, policymakers, partners, and stakeholders are encouraged to follow this guideline to implement IPC measures that protect healthcare workers and save lives. Additionally, investment in research to improve IPC responses for Ebola and Marburg disease is strongly recommended. 11. WHO acknowledges the contributions of various groups and individuals, including the core team, steering committee members, external reviewers, and collaborators, for their support in developing this guideline. Special thanks are extended to those who conducted systematic reviews, rapid evidence reviews, and contextual studies related to IPC measures for Ebola and Marburg diseases. 12. The guideline emphasizes the importance of cleaning, which physically removes microorganisms using water, detergents, and mechanical action. Cleaning is the first step in the decontamination process, which ensures objects are safe for handling, further processing, use, or disposal. 13. Contact transmission occurs through direct or indirect physical contact with an infected person or contaminated objects. Direct contact involves body-to-body transfer of microorganisms, such as touching blood or body fluids from an infected person. Indirect contact involves contaminated surfaces or objects, such as medical equipment or the environment. 14. Decontamination involves removing soil and pathogenic microorganisms from objects to make them safe. This process includes cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization. Disinfection reduces the number of viable microorganisms to a less harmful level but may not inactivate bacterial spores, prions, or some viruses. 15. Droplet transmission occurs when infectious droplets are generated by an infected person during coughing, sneezing, or talking. These droplets, containing microorganisms, are propelled through the air (usually less than 1 meter) and deposited on the mucous membranes of a susceptible host.
